PROVENANCE: every definition is original prose written for opsinjs; nothing is copied from the NHS A-Z or any other Crown-copyright source. `generatedAt` carries the token source hash rather than a build time, because this file is guarded by a byte-for-byte drift gate and a timestamp would fail it on every run.

terms.plain: sudden, or short-lasting
terms.reason: Often misread as 'severe'. It describes how quickly something started, not how bad it is.

terms.plain: taking a medicine the way it was prescribed
terms.reason: 'Compliance' frames the reader as obedient or not; 'adherence' is better but still clinical. Write what actually happened instead.

terms.plain: an unwanted effect of a medicine
terms.reason: 'Adverse' is not everyday English. 'Side effect' is understood, but it can make a serious effect sound minor, so say what the effect is.

terms.plain: not cancer
terms.reason: This word appears on reports and is one of the few whose plain meaning is genuinely reassuring, so the reader should be able to match the two.

terms.plain: something measurable in your body that says something about your health
terms.reason: Common in product copy, almost never understood outside research.

terms.plain: the pressure of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries, written as two numbers
terms.reason: The words are familiar but the two-number format is not. Always explain which number is which where both are shown.

terms.plain: a number worked out from your height and weight
terms.reason: The abbreviation is widespread and the calculation is not. Anywhere BMI is shown, say that it does not distinguish muscle from fat and is a poor guide for some people.

terms.plain: a slower than usual heart rate
terms.reason: Appears in device output. Also note that a slow resting heart rate is expected in many fit people.

terms.plain: a fatty substance carried in your blood
terms.reason: Widely known as a word, widely misunderstood as a single number. Most reports give several.

terms.plain: long-lasting, or ongoing
terms.reason: Often heard as 'severe'. It describes duration.

terms.plain: a reason this treatment is not safe for you
terms.reason: A word with no everyday equivalent that readers guess at. Never show it.

terms.plain: the pressure between heartbeats, which is the lower of the two blood pressure numbers
terms.reason: The reader's own record shows the clinical word, so both are needed to match them up.

terms.plain: an estimate of how well your kidneys are filtering
terms.reason: Appears on results with no explanation. The word 'estimated' matters and should never be dropped.

terms.plain: a result that says something was found when it was not there
terms.reason: Essential for interpreting any screening result honestly, and impossible to explain after the fact if the first screen did not mention it.

terms.plain: not eating or drinking anything except water for a set time before a test
terms.reason: Readers frequently assume water is included. Say the time and say that water is allowed.

terms.plain: your average blood sugar over about the last three months
terms.reason: One of the most common results a consumer app displays and one of the least understood. Also flag that it is reported in two different units worldwide.

terms.plain: one of the types of cholesterol measured in a blood test
terms.reason: Frequently described to readers as 'good cholesterol'. Avoid that shorthand: it invites the reader to treat one number as a verdict.

terms.plain: blood pressure that stays higher than the usual range
terms.reason: Frequently confused with 'tension' in the sense of stress.

terms.plain: blood sugar that has dropped below the range you were given
terms.reason: Time-critical. The reader may already know it as 'a hypo', and both forms must be recognisable.

terms.plain: inside the range this test uses for comparison
terms.reason: The replacement for 'normal'. Always name whose range it is: a laboratory's range, a device maker's range, or a range a clinician set for this person.

terms.plain: one of the types of cholesterol measured in a blood test
terms.reason: Usually captioned 'bad cholesterol'. Same objection as HDL: it turns one number into a moral judgement.

terms.plain: cancer
terms.reason: Never soften this and never show it without a route to a person. See /docs/health/emergency-and-escalation.

terms.plain: milligrams per decilitre, which is a unit used for blood test results
terms.reason: See mmol/L. Converting between the two is a correctness surface, not a display preference.

terms.plain: millimoles per litre, which is a unit used for blood test results
terms.reason: The same measurement is reported in mmol/L in some countries and mg/dL in others, and the numbers are not close. Never show a value without its unit.

terms.plain: swelling caused by fluid building up
terms.reason: Spelled two ways depending on country; the plain wording avoids the problem entirely.

terms.plain: outside the range this test uses for comparison
terms.reason: The replacement for 'abnormal'. It states a fact about a comparison and leaves the interpretation to whoever is entitled to make it.

terms.plain: what is likely to happen next
terms.reason: A word no component should ever need. If a product is showing a prognosis, a clinician wrote it.

terms.plain: the range a test result is compared against
terms.reason: The most important term in this glossary. A reference range is a comparison, not a target, and it belongs to a laboratory or a device rather than to the reader. Always name whose range it is and never call it a normal range.

terms.plain: a period when the signs of an illness have reduced or gone
terms.reason: Often heard as 'cured'. The plain wording keeps the distinction.

terms.plain: how many times your heart beats a minute when you are at rest
terms.reason: Understood as words but frequently confused with the heart rate shown during activity. Say when it was measured.

terms.plain: a test offered to people with no symptoms, to look for a possible problem early
terms.reason: Readers commonly assume a screening test is diagnostic. It is not, and the difference determines what the result means.

terms.plain: an estimate of how much oxygen your blood is carrying
terms.reason: Shown by consumer devices as a bare percentage. The word 'estimate' is not optional: the measurement is affected by movement, cold hands and skin tone, and the product must say so.

terms.plain: the pressure while your heart beats, which is the higher of the two blood pressure numbers
terms.reason: See diastolic.

terms.plain: a faster than usual heart rate
terms.reason: Appears in device output with no explanation and reliably alarms people.

terms.plain: changing a dose in small steps until it is right for you
terms.reason: No everyday equivalent; the plain wording is complete on its own.

terms.plain: a type of fat measured in a blood test
terms.reason: Appears on the same report as cholesterol and is routinely mistaken for it.

banned.reason: The counterpart of the same problem, and the version that frightens people.
Carries a verdict the system is not entitled to give.

banned.instead: say what the reading is and who can interpret it
banned.reason: opsinjs components never diagnose. Using the word implies they do.

banned.instead: state what the reading means and what happens next
banned.reason: Reassurance the system cannot back up, and it reads as a reason to worry.
Clinical register; means little to a lay reader, and it sounds like a verdict to the readers who do recognise it.
A reading is not a test the reader sat.

banned.instead: say the direction - higher, or lower
banned.reason: Moral framing of something largely outside the reader's control.
A verdict on a life, from one number. A reading can sit inside a range while the person is unwell, and outside it while they are fine.
'Just a bit high' minimises a reading the reader may need to act on.

banned.instead: the test did not find <what it looked for>
banned.reason: Same collision, in the other direction.

banned.instead: in the usual range, or the expected range for you
banned.reason: Outside a reference range is not abnormal in the everyday sense of the word, and inside one is not a clean bill of health. 'Normal' also carries a judgement about the person rather than about the reading. This word is banned outright across the system, including in code identifiers.
Sets up every future reading as a decline, in the register of a fitness tracker rather than a clinic.
Sets up every future reading as a decline.

banned.instead: lower than the range for you
banned.reason: Judges the person, not the measurement.
In everyday English 'positive' means good news. In a test result it usually means the opposite, and the collision is dangerous.

The same verdict in the other direction. Say which way the reading sits and against whose range; the replacement wording assumes the common case, so where the reading is low, say 'lower than the usual range'.
